title: The first plant that can stand in water
question: Does B read as reeds standing in a pond -- or as underwater weed? It is the emergent stems above the waterline I am unsure of, not the mechanism.
context_md:
Phase 1 of the aquatic plan: the pond stops being a dead blue rectangle.

Same bed, same seed, same binary -- the only difference is a switch (`PIXEL_PHYSICS_SUBMERGED_SHOOT`). Three frames each: 2,000 / 6,000 / 20,000. The waterline is the top of the blue; the pale band under it is the sediment a reed roots in.

**What I already measured, so you do not have to judge it:**

- It fires. 281 cells standing in the water at 20,000 frames against 4, and the tallest stem reaches 14 rows *above* the waterline.
- It does not drink the pond. The full water ledger (pond + soil + sky) is conserved to 0.09%; the pond itself settles at about 80% and holds from frame 6,000 on. A first version lost 56% of the pond and that was a real bug, now fixed.
- The palette is deliberately a different green from grass and foliage -- glaucous, blue-grey -- so a reed cannot read as a tall blade of grass.

**What I am unsure of, and why I am asking rather than tuning again:** the dense clump on the right reads to me more like pondweed than like a reed bed, and the stems wander rather than standing straight. I have already cut branching and reproduction once to get from a solid mat to this. I would rather have your eye than guess at a third setting.

items.label: A -- the pond as it ships today
items.caption: A plant in this pond germinates and never grows: the seedling sits on the sediment for the whole run.

items.label: B -- a plant that may cross the waterline
items.caption: The same bed with the reed's two new abilities: its shoot may enter water, and its seed sinks instead of floating.
